## B-209 — the `apelles` crate's own `--lib` test build stopped compiling, because sixteen test call sites did not follow `chroma_timeline_get` becoming `async`

status: **fixed** (2026-09-16, in D-338's pass) · severity: **high** (not a rendering defect — a *verification* one: `cargo test -p apelles --lib` failed at COMPILE time, so every one of that crate's 331 tests was unrunnable and nothing in it could be checked at all) · area: `app/src-tauri/src/chroma/project.rs` (test module)

- **found:** 2026-09-16, by the D-338 pass, on its first `cargo test -p apelles --lib` — 16 `error[E0599]: no method named 'unwrap' found for opaque type 'impl Future<…>'`. Pre-existing on `main` at `431bd22`; nothing in D-338 touched `project.rs`.
- **cause:** B-205/D-334 made `chroma_timeline_get` `pub async fn` + `spawn_blocking` (correctly — a `#[tauri::command]` without `async` runs on the UI thread, and that body does real blocking I/O). Its sixteen call sites in `project.rs`'s **test** module still called it synchronously, so they now `.unwrap()` a `Future`. The library itself compiles fine; only the test build breaks, which is why it shipped: a `cargo build`, a `cargo clippy` on the lib, and a `tauri dev` all stay green.
- **fix:** one `timeline_get()` helper in that test module, driving the command on a tiny `new_current_thread` runtime and `block_on` — the same pattern the module already used for the async `chroma_project_save`, rather than pulling `tokio::test` into an otherwise-sync test module. The tests are about what the command *persists*, not which thread it runs on, so they stay synchronous. `new_current_thread` still carries a blocking pool, which is what `spawn_blocking` needs.
- **verification:** `cargo test -p apelles --lib chroma::` → **331 passed, 0 failed**.
- **worth keeping in mind:** adding `async` to a `#[tauri::command]` is a source-compatible change for the *app* and a breaking one for every synchronous caller in a test. Nothing in the frontend or in a lib build can tell you; only the test build can, and only if someone runs it.

## B-208 — `scale` still means two different units in the two engines: a fraction of the output canvas in the export, the clip's native footprint in the composition in the preview

status: **fixed** (D-353, 2026-09-18) · severity: medium (silent, but bounded — the two coincide exactly whenever the clip's source resolution equals the project composition, which is the common case; `box_width`/`box_height` are the documented parity-safe alternative and were unaffected) · area: `app/src-tauri/src/chroma/edit.rs` (`ClipTransform::effective_size`) vs `packages/editor/src/timelineExport.ts` (`buildClipFilterChain`'s `widthExpr`)

- **found:** 2026-09-16, recorded inside B-201's own write-up. **Split out into its own entry by D-338**, which fixed B-201's *position* half — leaving an open paragraph inside a bug marked fixed is exactly the drift this file exists to prevent.
- **preview:** `scale` multiplies the clip's NATIVE pixel size mapped into composition space, so `scale = 1.0` means "this clip at its own size in the composition", not "fit to frame". A 1280×720 source in a 1920×1080 composition is two thirds of the frame wide at `scale = 1.0`.
- **export:** `widthExpr` is `${opts.width}*(${scaleExpr})` — a fraction of the output canvas outright. The same clip at `scale = 1.0` is the FULL frame wide.
- **why it has not bitten as hard as B-201 did:** the two are identical whenever `source resolution == composition`, which is every clip in every project built from one camera's footage at the project's own resolution. B-201's position divergence, by contrast, was wrong for *every* non-full-frame clip regardless of source size.
- **already documented rather than hidden** *(as filed — both of these texts were rewritten by the fix below)*: `timelineExport.ts` carries a comment on it ("whose meaning depends on the clip's own SOURCE resolution, which this pure, no-I/O module still cannot probe — B-074/D-184's own pre-existing, intentionally-not-reopened gap"), and `capabilities.json`'s `scale` entry now states both readings and points here instead of claiming `overlay_width = canvas_width * scale` "ALWAYS, in both".
- **why it is genuinely harder than B-201 was:** `timelineExport.ts` is a pure, no-I/O compiler — it cannot probe a source file's resolution, which is exactly what the preview's reading needs. Closing it means either feeding the compiler the media pool's already-probed dimensions (they exist; `editor_import_media` stores them) or changing the preview's `scale` to a canvas fraction, which would silently resize every existing clip that carries a non-default `scale`. Neither is a two-line edit, and unlike B-201 there is no external convention forcing the direction.
- **the parity test D-338 added is the place to extend when this is taken:** add a second named transform to the same pair, driven by `scale` on a source deliberately *not* the composition's size.
- **fixed by D-353 (2026-09-18), in the export, exactly as that decision called it.** `ClipTransform::effective_size` is untouched; `timelineExport.ts` learned the preview's reading instead. The mechanism is one new `TimelineExportOptions` field, `sourceFootprints` — each clip's own source resolution **as a fraction of the composition**, keyed by `Clip.id` — and `widthExpr` became `${opts.width}*${footprint.width}*(${scaleExpr})`. The compiler is still pure and still probes nothing: the dimensions were already probed at import and stored on the media-pool item, and `editorExport.ts`'s new `resolveSourceFootprints` just divides them by the composition size. A **fraction** rather than raw source pixels on purpose — that is what keeps `scale` resolution-independent, so exporting the same timeline at 720p still scales the whole layout uniformly instead of resizing one clip against the others.
- **the composition size had to be plumbed too, and that was the non-obvious half.** The compiler only ever knew the EXPORT's width/height, which is the composition only when nobody changes the resolution in the Export dialog. `packages/editor/src/compositionSize.ts` (new) is a one-shot warm/snapshot around `chroma_timeline_composition_size`, mirroring `textFonts.ts`/`captionMetrics.ts`/`gradeLuts.ts`' established "warm from the async entry point, read synchronously in the compiler" shape; `runEditorExport` and the Export dialog's enqueue both warm it. It **refetches on every warm** rather than caching once, because unlike a font catalogue this changes with `set_project_settings`. Unresolvable (an empty project with nothing to derive a size from) falls back to the export's own requested size — this compiler's own stated contract — rather than refusing, since that is a real reading of the document and not a dropped title or grade.
- **byte-identical for every project whose sources are the composition's size**, which is all of them until now: an absent entry, or a footprint of exactly `1`, emits the pre-fix `${opts.width}*(${scaleExpr})` string verbatim rather than `…*1*(…)`. Pinned by its own test.
- **`'stretch'` changed too, deliberately** (`fit_overrides`, an export-only knob): it now reads `scale` the same native-footprint way on BOTH axes, because `scale` has to mean one thing and `fit`/`stretch` must only decide where the HEIGHT comes from. For a source shaped like the canvas — `'stretch'`'s own stated main use — the box is still canvas-shaped exactly as before; it differs only for a source of a different shape.
- **verified by a genuinely non-degenerate parity case, which is the part this entry's own filing said was missing.** Three layers: (1) argv unit tests in `timelineExport.test.ts` (a half-composition source at `scale: 1` is half the frame, not all of it — plus the byte-identical, absent-entry, `box_width`-wins, `stretch` and keyframed-`scale` cases); (2) a real-ffmpeg pixel test, `'B-208/D-353 — scale parity with the live-preview compositor'` in `timelineExport.ffmpeg.test.ts` — a **160×120 source in a 320×240 canvas** at `scale 0.5`, asserting the 80×60 box `effective_size` computes and asserting BLACK where the old canvas-fraction reading painted; **confirmed to fail without the fix** and pass with it; (3) the decisive cross-engine one — a `c-scaled` clip (320×180 source, `scale: 0.5`, no `box_*`) added to D-350's `export-parity.json` harness, which `edit_render.rs` renders through the **real Rust compositor** and the real filter graph and diffs pixel for pixel. That fixture used to generate every source at the composition's size *specifically to keep this divergence out of it*, and said so; it now carries per-source sizes.
- **the two same-canvas parity tests either side of it could not have caught this**, which is worth keeping written down: a source at exactly the canvas's size, or a box spelled in `box_width`/`box_height`, is the one geometry where both readings are the same number.
- **two pieces of pre-existing MCP drift fell out of this and are fixed here too.** Changing the `scale` capability text meant re-capturing the parity corpus (`crates/apelles-mcp/parity/capture.py`), and the corpus in the tree turned out to predate D-350's `renderer` parameter entirely — so the gate had been comparing an `editor_export` that no longer existed, and was hiding two real divergences between the two MCP surfaces. Both are now closed: (1) the Rust `editor_export` docstring's `renderer` paragraph was wrapped differently from `mcp/server.py`'s, which the gate compares byte-for-byte ("a reflow is a change") — rewrapped to match, same words; (2) `renderer` was typed `Option<String>` in Rust against Python's `ExportRenderer = Literal["filter", "compositor"]`, so the published `inputSchema` silently dropped the two-value `enum` an agent relies on — there is now a real `ExportRenderer` enum in `crates/apelles-mcp/src/schemas.rs`, mirroring the `FitMode` pattern beside it. `cargo test -p apelles-mcp --test parity` goes 4-passed-1-failed → **5/5**.
- **found while building that fixture case, and deliberately NOT swept under the fix:** the first version of it used a source SMALLER than the composition (320×180 in 640×360) and the pixel comparison failed — not on geometry. A pixel dump showed both engines placing the box's bottom edge on exactly the same row (yellow through y=179, base from y=180 in both); the whole difference was a 4-row soft-edge/chroma band straddling that boundary, per-channel deltas of 25-27 against the harness's own 24 threshold, which a 3×3 erosion cannot thin away. Cause: the render path decodes an UNDERSIZED source up to the composition's size and then composites it back down into the box, so that clip pays two resamples and lands a softer edge than ffmpeg's single `scale`. Small, pre-existing, and nothing to do with `scale`'s units — so the fixture case was moved to an OVERSIZED source (1280×720 at `scale: 0.25`, footprint 2.0), which goes down the same single-resample path as every other clip in the harness and is the commoner real shape besides. The tolerance was NOT loosened. Worth a look of its own if undersized sources ever matter for export quality.

## B-202 — a `motion_render` that fails partway through reports the failure NOWHERE: the loop stops, the op has already timed out, and nothing is logged

status: **fixed** (2026-09-19, **D-359**) · severity: medium (no data loss — but a partial render is indistinguishable from a slow one, and the reason is unrecoverable after the fact) · area: `packages/motion/src/useMotionManifest.ts` (the per-scene render loop) + `app/src-tauri/src/chroma/control.rs`'s 20s `BRIDGE_TIMEOUT`

- **found:** 2026-09-16, during D-333, rendering a four-scene manifest. Hit twice.
- **the three behaviours are each individually reasonable and combine badly.** (1) `motion_render` renders one file per scene SEQUENTIALLY and, by deliberate design (D-180), a scene's failure **stops the loop** rather than skipping — "the owner needs to know exactly which scene failed and why." (2) A multi-scene render always exceeds `control.rs`'s hardcoded 20s bridge timeout, so the caller gets a 504 and the eventual `respond(...)` "emits into an event nobody listens for any more" — a documented, accepted no-op (`useMotionControl.ts`'s own module doc). (3) The failure is surfaced only as frontend React state (`renderError`) and the partial `results` array.
- **net effect:** the caller who was told to treat the 504 as "inconclusive, check the output on disk" finds N of M files and **no error anywhere** — not in the op reply (already timed out), not in the app log (nothing is written), not in `motion_get_state` (which reports no render status at all). The only signal is arithmetic on a directory listing, and it cannot distinguish "still rendering", "stopped on a failure", and "finished early".
- **observed:** a directory with 3 of 4 scenes and no running `remotion` process, twice, with an empty app log. Both times the individual scene rendered perfectly when driven directly (`npx remotion render … --frames=840-1139`), so the stopping cause was environmental (a competing render contending for the bundler), which is exactly the sort of transient the missing error message would have named instantly.
- **fix, smallest first:** log the render error and the failing scene id server-side when the loop aborts, so a timed-out caller has somewhere to look. Better: expose render status (`idle`/`running`/`error`, the failing `sceneId`, the error, and how many scenes are done) on `motion_get_state`, which is already the tab's polling read and already reports `loadState`/`saveError`. That also gives a caller real progress instead of counting files. Raising `BRIDGE_TIMEOUT` is NOT the fix — a long render will always outlive any timeout worth having.
- **fixed (D-359) — both halves this entry asked for, and the structural reason the first one was missing.**
  - **`motion_get_state` now carries a `render` block**: `state` (`idle`/`running`/`error`), `scenesTotal`/`scenesDone`/`doneSceneIds`, `sceneId` (the one rendering right now) and `failedSceneId` + `error`. All three of the states this entry says a directory listing cannot tell apart are now distinguishable in one call, and `doneSceneIds` is exactly what is on disk (the loop stops at the failure, so there is nothing after it). `BRIDGE_TIMEOUT` is untouched, deliberately, for the reason stated above.
  - **`chroma_motion_render` logs** the render's start (scene, frame range, destination) and, on failure, `render FAILED — scene <id>: <error>` — covering both the `run_render` failure and the staging→destination `rename` failure. That is the floor this entry asked for: whatever a caller does or does not poll, the app log now names the scene.
  - **the root cause of "surfaced only as frontend React state" was that the loop was not a value.** It lived inside `useMotionManifest`'s `render()` `useCallback`, so its progress could not be read from outside the component and could not be tested at all in `@apelles/motion` (that package's vitest environment is `node` — no jsdom, no react-dom), which is why it shipped with no coverage of the failure path. The loop is now `renderLoop.ts`'s pure `runSceneRenders`; the hook is the shell around it. D-180's "a failure STOPS the loop" is unchanged and is now pinned by a test.
  - **the GUI half, same value:** the Render button reads `Rendering 2/4…`, and the error line reads `render failed (scene <id>): …` instead of just `render failed`.
  - **regression tests:** `packages/motion/src/renderLoop.test.ts` (11 cases — the failing scene names itself in the final status, the loop stops rather than skipping, progress is monotonic, a finished run is `idle` with every scene counted, an `onRendered` throw never fails a succeeded render) plus two in `motionOps.test.ts` that drive the REAL loop with a deliberately-failing scene and read the answer back out of `motion_get_state` — the end-to-end claim this entry is about, rather than a hand-written status literal.

## B-204 — a clip shorter than the prefetch lookahead has its own decode-pipe standby evicted by the clip AFTER it, so its cut pays the full respawn it was meant to hide

status: **fixed** (D-334, 2026-09-15) · severity: medium (a visible hitch at a subset of cuts on a heavily recut timeline; never a wrong picture) · area: `crates/apelles-media/src/decode_pipe.rs` (`PipePool::standby`, `prefetch` → `sync_prefetch`), `app/src-tauri/src/chroma/edit.rs` (`upcoming_boundary_targets`)

- **found:** 2026-09-15, by reading D-324's own implementation against the shape of the owner's real recut `2026-09-12-c040` — 75 clips, of which **7 are shorter than the 12-frame (0.5 s at 24 fps) lookahead**, the shortest a single frame.
- **the mechanism, confirmed in code and then by test:** D-324 held at most ONE standby per `PipeSlot` and resolved the timeline at a single instant, `pos + lookahead`. For a clip `N+1` whose duration is less than the lookahead, the layer resolved at that instant is already clip `N+2` *while playback is still approaching `N+1`* — so `prefetch` replaced `N+1`'s standby with `N+2`'s before `N+1` was ever reached. `N+1`'s boundary then paid a full keyframe seek **and** the eviction wasted an `ffmpeg` doing it. Compounding it, `playback_frame_scaled` dropped any standby that could not serve the frame in hand, which is `N+2`'s standby at `N+1`'s boundary — so the following clip's prefetch was destroyed too.
- **cost of the seek being paid, measured on that source** (3840×2160 HEVC → 960 px, videotoolbox, 16 of the project's own cut points): median **723 ms** time-to-first-frame, min 460, max 2372. Sequential reads either side are 6.8 ms.
- **not the cause of the owner's main complaint, and D-334 says so.** The measured session had median 200 ms/frame with only 3 cuts and no short clips in the window; that median is **B-146**. This entry is the hitches (p95 620 ms), not the baseline.
- **fixed by** making `standby` a list per slot (cap 3), replacing `prefetch(one boundary)` with the declarative `sync_prefetch(wanted)` so releasing is the scheduler's single call rather than a guess made at decode time, and walking the whole lookahead window for a CHAIN of boundaries instead of sampling one instant. Pinned by `decode_pipe::tests::a_chain_of_short_clip_boundaries_all_stay_primed_and_each_is_adopted` and `chroma::edit::preview_throughput_tests::a_run_of_clips_shorter_than_the_lead_keeps_its_chain_primed`.
- **found in passing, same fix:** `upcoming_boundary_targets` clamped its target to `max(clip.start_frame, pos)`, which is one frame BEHIND the live pipe by the time `prime` runs (it runs after the frame is decoded, so `next_index` is already `source_frame + 1`). So every ordinary mid-clip frame spawned a standby that could never be adopted and was killed a frame later — against the module doc's explicit "one extra timeline walk per frame and no processes". Measured to cost nothing (a spawn-and-kill per frame beside a live sequential read moved its median 7.13 → 6.62 ms), so it was waste rather than the stutter; fixed anyway, and pinned by `a_mid_clip_playback_frame_primes_nothing`, which asserts **zero** standbys where D-324's own test asserted `<= 1` and so could not catch it.

## B-203 — `box_width`/`box_height` can be SET and are persisted, but `editor_get_timeline` omits them, so the only parity-safe sizing mechanism cannot be read back

status: **fixed** (2026-09-18) · severity: medium (nothing renders wrong — but an agent cannot verify the one transform field it is supposed to prefer, and the natural check returns a false negative) · area: `packages/editor/src/useEditorControl.ts` (`editor_get_timeline`'s clip serialization)

- **found:** 2026-09-16, during D-333, while verifying full-frame overlay placement.
- **repro:** `editor_set_clip_transform(track, clip, box_width: 1, box_height: 1)` → `{ok: true}`. Then `editor_get_timeline` and look at that clip. The returned clip object contains `opacity`, `positionX`, `positionY`, `scale`, `rotation`, `cropLeft/Top/Right/Bottom`, `fadeIn*`, `volume`, `pan`, `keyframes` — and **no `boxWidth`/`boxHeight` key at all**. The string `boxWidth` does not appear anywhere in `packages/`, `app/src` or `crates/`.
- **the write side is fine.** `save_project` then reading `project.json` shows `"box_width": 1.0, "box_height": 1.0` on the clip, exactly as set. The Rust `Clip` has the fields (`crates/apelles-timeline/src/lib.rs`), `timeline.ts`'s `applyOp` assigns them (`nc.box_width = op.box_width`), and both compositors consume them. Only the read model drops them.
- **why this bites harder than it looks:** `box_width`/`box_height` are, per `capabilities.json`'s own advice and B-201, the ONLY size mechanism with real preview/export parity — `scale` means different things in the two engines. So the field an agent is steered toward is precisely the one it cannot confirm through the API it is told to confirm with. The natural verification (set it, read it back) reads as "my write silently did nothing", which is what happened here: the write had worked all along.
- **it is an omission, not a wrong value.** A `jq` projection asking for `boxWidth` yields `null` because the key is absent, which is easy to misread as "stored as null". Worth stating explicitly since that misreading costs a debugging cycle.
- **fixed:** `timelineDto` (`useEditorControl.ts`) now reports `boxWidth: c.box_width ?? null` / `boxHeight: c.box_height ?? null` alongside the other transform fields — `null`, not `0`/`1`, for "no override," the same explicit-null convention every other nullable field on this DTO already uses (`linkGroup`, `text`) and the one the stored field's own doc comment requires (a cleared override round-trips as `null`, not a missing key).
- **confirmed genuinely a single-site fix:** both MCP surfaces were checked, not assumed. `mcp/server.py`'s `get_timeline()` is `json.dumps(_op("editor_get_timeline"), ...)` — no field allowlist. `crates/apelles-mcp/src/tools/edit.rs`'s `get_timeline()` calls `self.op("editor_get_timeline", ...)` and renders the raw envelope (`render::json_text`) — same shape, no allowlist. Both are pure passthroughs over `timelineDto`'s own output, so neither needed a change. (Their docstrings already omitted several other existing DTO fields too — e.g. `positionX`/`scale`/`crop*`/`keyframes`/`text` — a pre-existing, separate gap this fix does not extend.)
- **verified:** new `packages/editor/src/useEditorControl.test.ts` (`timelineDto` now exported test-only) — 4 cases: a set override round-trips, an unset clip reports `boxWidth`/`boxHeight` present-and-`null` (not omitted, not `0`/`1`), an explicitly-cleared override (`box_width: null`) still reads back `null`, and one axis overridden independently of the other. `npm test --workspace @apelles/editor` and `npx tsc --noEmit -p packages/editor` both clean.

## B-201 — `position_x`/`position_y` mean a CENTRE OFFSET in the live preview but the TOP-LEFT CORNER in the export, so any non-full-width overlay lands in two different places

status: **fixed** (2026-09-16, **D-338**) · severity: **high** (silent — both engines render confidently, and they disagree by `(1 - box_width)/2` of the canvas; a half-width overlay verified in the preview exports 960px away at 3840 wide) · area: `app/src-tauri/src/chroma/edit.rs` (`composite_layer_onto`) vs `packages/editor/src/timelineExport.ts` (`buildClipFilterChain`)

- **fixed by D-338:** the PREVIEW moved to the export's TOP-LEFT convention — both placement computations in `composite_layer_onto` are now `x = position_x * cw`, `y = position_y * ch`, with the layer's own size out of the placement entirely, and `transformGeometry.ts`'s `clipBoxFraction` (the drawn box, and via `canvasPick.ts` the click hit-rect) dropped the matching `0.5 - size/2` term. The export was left alone deliberately: `overlay`'s top-left reading is ffmpeg's own external convention and is what `capabilities.json`'s stacked comparison recipe and the `chroma-comparison-reel` skill depend on. See D-338 for the options and the three knock-on consequences (titles provably unaffected, `scale` now growing about the top-left in both engines, the corner drag writing a compensating `position`).
- **no data migration was written, and the audit says why:** every `.chroma` project under `~/Movies/Chroma` was re-read clip by clip. Exactly two clips carry non-default geometry, both in the old, unrelated `2026-09-09-edit` — one renders byte-identically (a full-frame source, where the two conventions coincide), and one (`scale 0.8583` at `position 0,0`) genuinely moves from centred to flush-top-left. Its equivalent new-convention placement is `position_x = position_y = 0.070827`, written down in D-338 rather than fixed by a migration pass that would exist for one number in one project. Both `-mgfx` projects and both `c038`/`c040` cuts are entirely default and unaffected.
- **the missing test this entry called the real root cause now exists**, as a deliberately duplicated pair — `composite_layer_onto_agrees_with_the_exporter_on_the_parity_rectangle` (`edit.rs`) and `'D-338/B-201 — placement parity with the live-preview compositor'` (`timelineExport.ffmpeg.test.ts`) — both rendering `box_width/box_height 0.5` at `position 0.25, 0.25` onto a 320×240 canvas and both asserting the same hard-coded rectangle, `x ∈ [80, 240)`, `y ∈ [60, 180)`.
- **deliberately NOT closed here:** the separate `scale` unit divergence this entry also records is now **B-208**, with its own entry, rather than an open paragraph inside a bug marked fixed.
- **D-333's workaround is lifted.** The eight motion-graphics overlays in `2026-09-12-c038-mgfx` and `2026-09-12-c040-mgfx` no longer sit full-frame: all eight are now `box_width`/`box_height` `0.35` at `position 0.03, 0.06` — an upper-left inset card over the dark, empty side of the shot, sized once for both so the two videos share one overlay language, and chosen against the real frames rather than guessed (the subject is centred in both, plant right, dark door left). Nothing was exported.
- **a live demonstration of the bug, worth keeping:** those same stored numbers, screenshotted through the pre-fix build still running at the time (`scratch/d338-c040-stored-values-on-OLD-build.png`), land the card squarely over the speaker's face — displaced by exactly `(1 - 0.35)/2 = 0.325` of the canvas on each axis, the divergence this entry predicts. The intended placement was captured by temporarily writing the old convention's equivalent value (`position −0.295, −0.265`), which makes the pre-fix compositor draw precisely the rectangle the fixed one draws for `0.03, 0.06`: `scratch/d338-c038-inset-preview.png` and `scratch/d338-c040-inset-preview.png`.

- **found:** 2026-09-16, by the D-333 audit, while working out where to place a half-frame motion-graphics overlay. Code reading plus the two engines' own tests, not a live visual report — which is precisely why it has survived: nothing crashes and each side is self-consistent.
- **preview (Rust):** `x = cw/2 - ww/2 + position_x * cw` — `position_x = 0` means CENTRED. Its own unit test `composite_layer_onto_respects_position_offset` asserts exactly this, and `packages/editor/src/transformGeometry.ts` mirrors it (`left: 0.5 - width/2 + position.x`) so the GUI's on-canvas transform box agrees with the preview.
- **export (ffmpeg):** `overlay=x='<position_x>*W'` — ffmpeg's `overlay` x is the overlay's TOP-LEFT corner, so `position_x = 0` means LEFT-ALIGNED. Its real-ffmpeg test `timelineExport.ffmpeg.test.ts` stacks the bottom clip of a comparison layout with `position_y: 0.5`, which only works under the top-left reading.
- **the divergence is exactly `(1 - box_fraction)/2` per axis**, so it vanishes at full width/height and is worst at small overlays. That is why it has never been caught: the one case anyone verified end to end was full-frame.
- **the capabilities document is wrong about this**, which makes it worse than an undocumented gap — `crates/apelles-mcp/src/tools/edit/capabilities.json`'s `position_and_crop_units` states "0,0 = top-left" unconditionally, and its `scale` entry claims `overlay_width = canvas_width * scale` "ALWAYS, in both the live preview and export". Both are true of the export only. An agent that reads the capabilities doc and trusts it will author for the wrong engine.
- **`scale` diverges the same way, separately:** in the preview it multiplies the clip's NATIVE pixel size mapped into composition space (so `scale = 1.0` is 1:1 native, not fit-to-frame); in the export it is a fraction of canvas width. `timelineExport.ts` acknowledges this one in a comment ("whose meaning depends on the clip's own SOURCE resolution, which this pure, no-I/O module still cannot probe — B-074/D-184's own pre-existing, intentionally-not-reopened gap"). `box_width`/`box_height` are canvas fractions in BOTH and are the only size mechanism with real parity today.
- **worked around, not fixed, by D-333:** those motion-graphics overlays were placed full-frame (`box_width`/`box_height` = 1.0 at position 0,0), the one geometry where the two engines agree exactly. Flagged as a workaround rather than presented as done, per CLAUDE.md.
- **why it was not fixed there:** it is one term on either side (`+ (1 - w)/2` in the export's overlay expression, or `- cw/2 + ww/2` in `composite_layer_onto`), but the blast radius is real in both directions and belongs to the owner, not to a motion-graphics task. Changing the EXPORT breaks the stacked full-width/half-height comparison recipe that `capabilities.json` documents and that the `chroma-comparison-reel` skill depends on. Changing the PREVIEW breaks the GUI's on-canvas drag, `transformGeometry.ts`, and the stored transform of every existing project.
- **fix, when taken:** pick one convention, change the other side, update `capabilities.json` (which is currently wrong either way), and add a real parity test that renders the SAME non-full-width transform through both engines and compares — the missing test is the actual root cause here. Note B-088's own write-up records that the one live stacking comparison was made against a stale preview, so the two engines have never actually been compared on the same frame.
## B-207 — three Tauri commands on the project-open path ran INLINE ON THE UI THREAD, so opening a project genuinely froze the window rather than merely being slow

status: **fixed** (2026-09-16) · severity: high (this is the "app becomes unresponsive" half of the owner's report, and it is a different and worse class of defect than the slow-but-async work around it — a blocked UI thread cannot paint, cannot scroll, and cannot cancel) · area: `app/src-tauri/src/chroma/edit.rs`, `app/src-tauri/src/chroma/project.rs`, D-334

- **found:** 2026-09-16, chasing the owner's report that "opening a project takes forever ... and app becomes unresponsive". The wording mattered: "slow" and "unresponsive" are different failures, and conflating them would have sent the whole investigation after throughput when the freeze is a threading bug. Found by auditing which commands on the open path lack the `async` keyword.
- **cause:** Tauri's own documentation states it plainly — "**commands without the _async_ keyword are executed on the main thread**" (https://v2.tauri.app/develop/calling-rust/). Three commands on the open path were declared `pub fn`, not `pub async fn`, and all three do real blocking work:
  - `chroma_timeline_get` (`edit.rs`) — the worst of them. Reads and parses the project manifest **uncached** (212 KB of JSON on the owner's real `2026-09-12-c040`), runs every schema migration, back-fills legacy positions across all 150 clips, and may write the manifest back out. It also re-fires **on every window focus**, so the freeze was not even limited to opening.
  - `chroma_project_list` (`project.rs`) — scans the whole projects directory, `load_manifest`s every project found, then reads and base64-encodes each one's `thumb.jpg`. O(projects) file I/O paid inline at launcher mount, i.e. the very first thing the app does.
  - `chroma_session_list` (`session.rs`) — audited and deliberately **left alone**: its body is `snapshot()`, a clone of the shot vec with no I/O. Recorded here so the next reader knows it was checked rather than missed.
- **fix:** the two real offenders became `async` **and** moved their bodies onto `spawn_blocking`. `async` alone would have been the wrong fix and is worth stating: it only moves the work to a tokio runtime worker, which the synchronous blocking I/O would then block instead — starving every other async command rather than the UI thread. `spawn_blocking` is what a synchronous body actually needs.
- **not claimed:** this does not make opening fast. It makes opening *not freeze the window*, which is a separate property. The throughput half is D-334's other fixes (B-206, the grade batch, the thumbnail cache).
- **worth keeping in mind:** the `async` keyword on a `#[tauri::command]` is load-bearing and invisible at the call site — nothing in the frontend, and no test, can tell a main-thread command from an off-thread one. Both fixed commands now carry a comment saying so, because the next person to touch them has nothing else to warn them.

## B-206 — every clip on a track fetched its audio waveform whether or not it was on screen, so opening a 150-clip project asked the backend for 75 audio decodes to fill a viewport showing five

status: **fixed** (2026-09-16) · severity: high (the dominant cost of "opening a project takes forever" and "timeline takes forever" on a real recut project) · area: `packages/editor/src/Waveform.tsx`, `packages/editor/src/TimelinePane.tsx`, D-334

- **found:** 2026-09-16, measured rather than guessed, with a new counting harness (`TimelinePane.mountCost.dom.test.tsx`) built specifically because the existing `playheadCost` harness stubs `chroma_audio_waveform` to `[]` — correct for ITS question (React overhead), and exactly what hid this one.
- **cause:** two facts that are each fine alone and bad together. (1) The timeline library `@xzdarcy/react-timeline-editor` virtualizes **rows** vertically (a `react-virtualized` `Grid` with `columnCount={1}`) but does **not** virtualize **actions** horizontally at all — `edit_row.tsx` maps every action in a row unconditionally, so every clip on a track is mounted no matter where the viewport is scrolled. (2) `Waveform`'s fetch effect therefore ran for every clip. `Filmstrip` had defended itself against exactly this since D-128 (`requestWindow` returns `null` for an off-screen clip — "what stops a 40-clip timeline from requesting 40 windows when two are visible"); `Waveform` never got the same treatment, and that asymmetry is the bug.
- **measured, before:** on the owner's real project shape (75 linked A/V pairs = 150 clips, one 686 s 4K source), a mount fired **75** `chroma_audio_waveform` calls; at 150 pairs (300 clips), **150**. Exactly linear in clip count. Each one is a real `symphonia` decode on a cold cache, and the backend had **no concurrency bound on them at all**.
- **measured, after:** **5** at 150 clips and **5** at 300 clips — constant, bounded by what the viewport can actually show, against 4 for an 8-clip timeline that genuinely does fit on screen. Total mount IPC 155 → 10 at 300 clips.
- **fix:** the on-screen test moved into a shared `clipVisibility.ts` (`isClipVisible`) and both `Filmstrip` and `Waveform` now call it; `TimelinePane` passes the visible slice to **both** waveforms.
- **a real trap this hit, recorded because it would have shipped a half-fix:** wiring only the video track's waveform changed nothing measurable. An A/V-linked pair resolves to a **single shared** `(path, start, duration, buckets)` cache key, so the audio track's ungated fetch still covered the whole fan-out — the after-number stayed at 75 until the audio-track waveform was gated too. The harness caught it; reading the diff would not have.
- **also caught, in the harness itself:** two separate ways this test passed for the wrong reason — a module-level peak cache leaking between cases (understating the fan-out), and then a remount measuring `0 -> 0` and satisfying a "not many" assertion vacuously. Both fixed, and the test now asserts the small case fetched something real before comparing. A culling fix is exactly the kind of change that makes a counting test vacuous.
- **left open, deliberately:** the backend still caches waveform peaks **per clip range** (`source_key` + start + duration), so a cold open of a heavily recut project still pays one decode per *visible* clip rather than one per *source*. Premiere's `.pek` peak files are per-file, not per-clip ("PEK files are created for all audio-containing files on import", https://helpx.adobe.com/premiere/desktop/organize-media/import-files/audio-conforming-specifications.html), and the machinery to do the same here already exists (`rebucket_peaks` re-slices an envelope for free). Named in `docs/04-roadmap.md` rather than done in this pass.

## B-200 — `debug_record_video`'s `width` silently did nothing, because `snapshotWidth` is in POINTS and it was being handed pixels

status: **fixed** (2026-09-16) · severity: medium (nothing was wrong in the output file — but the parameter whose entire job is to keep the recorder from perturbing the app it records was inert, so every recording cost ~4x what it should and the number burned into it was correspondingly further from the truth) · area: `app/src-tauri/src/chroma/debug_record.rs`, D-330

- **found:** 2026-09-16, on the recorder's very FIRST live run, by reading the result's own reported numbers rather than trusting the parameter. The reply came back `width: 2560, height: 1440` — the native backing size — despite a default `width` of 1280, with `captureMsMedian: 58.73` and 6 of 75 frames padded because the capture could not hold a 15fps cadence.
- **expected:** `width: 1280` produces a 1280-pixel-wide recording.
- **actual:** the setting had no effect whatsoever; every recording was full native resolution.
- **cause:** `WKSnapshotConfiguration.snapshotWidth` is expressed in **points**, not pixels. The window here is 1280 points wide, so asking for "1280" requested exactly its existing width — and on a 2x display that rasterises at 2560 real pixels. The value was being passed through verbatim on the assumption that the two units were the same. Nothing errors in this situation; WebKit honours the request precisely, and the request happens to mean "no change".
- **fix:** `debug_record::snapshot_width` now takes the window's scale factor and divides by it, so the argument means the output video's real pixel width — which is the unit a caller recording a video is actually thinking in, and the only one they can specify without knowing the display's scale. Unit-tested (`the_requested_width_is_output_pixels_converted_into_snapshot_points`) including the degenerate scale factors, since the failure mode is silent. `debug_capture::capture_webview_raw`'s own doc now states the unit explicitly at the point the value crosses into WebKit.
- **verification:** re-measured on the same instance, same project, same 5s duration — **2560x1440 / 58.73ms median / 69 captured + 6 padded** before, **1280x720 / 15.0ms median / 75 captured + 0 padded** after. A 3.9x reduction in what each capture costs the app being recorded, and the target cadence now fully sustained.
- **worth keeping in mind:** this is precisely the class of defect D-330's tooling exists to catch — a plausible-looking number that is not what it claims to be — and it was caught only because the tool reports what it actually did rather than echoing what it was asked for. Had `debug_record_video` returned just `{ok: true, path}`, it would have shipped.

## B-199 — the transport bar's `current / total` timecode visibly jittered the rest of the transport on every frame tick

status: **fixed** (2026-09-15) · severity: low (cosmetic — nothing was mis-seeked or mis-measured, but a readout that visibly nudges every tick reads as a bug and drew attention away from the numbers themselves) · area: `packages/player/src/Player.tsx`

- **found:** 2026-09-15, live, by the owner, from a screenshot of the transport bar mid-playback.
- **cause:** the readout already had `tabular-nums`, which fixes DIGIT advance widths — but only digits. `fmtTimecode`'s colons and the `" / "` separator still rode the app's normal proportional UI font, whose non-digit glyphs are not guaranteed identical width across every digit combination. `fmtTimecode` itself always returns exactly `HH:MM:SS:FF` (fixed length, zero-padded), so the STRING never changed length — the drift was sub-pixel glyph-metric noise, small but visible every single tick.
- **first attempt, also wrong:** wrapping each half in its own `width: 11ch` box (one box per `HH:MM:SS:FF` half) assumed `1ch` in this font equals one monospace-digit's rendered width. It does not — `ch` is defined off the font's `"0"` glyph, which is narrower here than the tabular-nums digit advance actually renders at, so each box came out wider than its content and `text-align: right` pushed the gap to the LEFT of each half instead of removing it — a worse, more visible bug (a large gap between `/` and the second timecode) than the one being fixed. Caught immediately from the owner's next screenshot, reverted.
- **fix:** `font-mono` (a real fixed-pitch stack) on the whole readout. In a true monospace font every character — digit, colon, space, slash — has the same advance width by construction, so the entire string's rendered width is a true constant with no explicit width/`ch` arithmetic needed at all.
- **folded into the same change, a real request, not a bug:** the owner also asked to drop the trailing `:FF` frame field from this specific readout ("we do not need to show the milliseconds at all") — `fmtTimecode` itself is untouched (the marker popover and every other caller still need exact frame round-tripping); only this display strips it, via `dropFrameField`, a plain string slice, since nothing else needs a frameless variant yet.
- **verification:** `tsc` clean on `packages/player`; live-checked in the real running app (screenshot before/after) — `00:00:56:21 / 00:04:11:19` (jittering, frame field shown) → `00:01:10 / 00:04:11` (stable width, no frame field).

## B-198 — retake detection missed a line the speaker said three times, because Whisper's segment boundaries do not line up with the restart boundaries

status: fixed (2026-09-15, **D-327**) · severity: medium (a silent false negative — the detector reported success and simply did not propose ~22s of duplicated speech, so a reviewer had no signal anything was missing) · area: `crates/apelles-speech/src/retake.rs`

- **found:** 2026-09-15, live, on the owner's own footage (`A001_09122356_C040.MOV`, transcript 142-180s). The speaker stumbles and restarts one line **three times** in a row — plainly audible as a triple repeat — and `editor_detect_retakes` reported a single group of two, covering 142.38-157.48s and nothing after it.
- **cause, confirmed by measurement rather than reading:** not a threshold or a scoring bug. `detect_retakes` compared one transcript utterance against one other, and Whisper segments on its own acoustic/length heuristics with no idea a restart happened — so **its boundaries straddle the repeats**. Segment #3 alone held the tail of one delivery concatenated with the head of the next. Across all fifteen pairs of the six segments the best score was 0.857 (#0 vs #2, the one pair that did group) and **every pair involving the two segments carrying repeats two and three scored 0.18-0.28**. The repeated material was never inside any single string the detector compared, so no threshold could have found it.
- **not the diagnosis it looks like.** The obvious reading is "edit distance is lexical, use a semantic model." That was built (`all-MiniLM-L6-v2`, on-device ONNX) and **measured, then rejected**: cosine ranks a sentence against its own negation at 0.946 and an antonym pair at 0.981, *above* every genuine retake in this footage (0.59-0.77). Five of six must-not-group probes outscored the weakest true retake — no threshold separates them. Edit distance ranks the same negation pair at 0.843, correctly *below* real retakes. Numbers and method: `docs/notes/retake-detection.md`.
- **fix (D-327):** the unit of comparison is now a **span** of up to `max_span_utterances` (default 3) adjacent utterances joined into one string, so a repeat that straddles boundaries lands inside a comparable string. The same material scores **0.905** as spans. A group now reports `takes` (inclusive ranges over its `members`) and `keep` indexes `takes`. Two new guards came with it — `min_words` counts DISTINCT words (three joined "Yeah."s otherwise clear a total-word bar) and a span may only be glued if every utterance in it shares >=50% of its vocabulary with the anchor (otherwise `containment` sweeps an aside into a take, and then into a cut).
- **verification:** the real six segments are a regression test in `retake.rs`. Before: one group, members `[0, 2]`, coverage stops at 157.48s. After: one group, **three takes**, members `[0, 2, 3, 4]`, coverage reaches 179.92s, keeper is the last delivery, and segment #5 (which has moved on to self-attention) is still correctly excluded. `max_span_utterances: 1` reproduces the old result exactly and is pinned by its own test so the two are readable side by side.
- **knock-on defect fixed in the same pass, never reported but real:** the Recut panel and `retakeEnvelope` (the MCP op) each built one cut candidate per *member* and treated `keep` as a member index. That was correct only while every take was one utterance. With multi-utterance takes it would have offered half a delivery for cutting while marking the other half the keeper — i.e. it would have eaten words the speaker meant to keep. Both now go through one shared `groupTakes()`.
- **known limit, deliberately not fixed, pinned by its own test:** delivery two begins *inside* segment #2 and delivery three *inside* segment #3, so a take made of whole utterances cannot claim the fragment "just under waves it." for delivery one without also claiming the next delivery's material. The detector leaves it out — under-cutting rather than over-cutting, the safe direction for a detector that only proposes (D-318). Word-accurate take boundaries need per-word timings through the bridge; see `docs/04-roadmap.md`.

## B-197 — `editor_ripple_delete_ranges` silently drops some ranges from a larger batch while reporting full success

status: **fixed** (**D-361**, 2026-09-19) · severity: high (a caller had no way to know some accepted cuts were never actually applied — the tool reported `"ranges": N` matching the input count regardless) · area: `packages/editor/src/timeline.ts` (`ripple_delete_ranges` reducer case, `rippleDeleteOneRange`), `useEditorControl.ts`, `RecutPanel.tsx`

- **found:** 2026-09-15, live — a 87-range combined cut (60 previously-verified-working ranges from an earlier successful 60-range apply on this exact source file, plus 27 newly-found silence/retake ranges) applied to a fresh single clip of `A001_09122356_C040.MOV` (16,475 source frames). The call returned `{"ok": true, "ranges": 87}` — the same success shape a working call reports — but the resulting timeline was **630 frames (26.25s) longer than the arithmetic union of the 87 ranges implies**, and `88` clips came out where `87` were expected (one *fewer* cut boundary than requested).
- **confirmed, not guessed:** brute-forced the true frame-level union of the 87 sent ranges (9522 frames) against the actual resulting clip list's source-frame coverage. Exactly **two** of the 87 ranges were **not applied at all** — `{start: 6806, end: 6961}` (155 frames) and `{start: 11524, end: 12003}` (479 frames), 634 frames total, matching the observed discrepancy almost exactly (the remaining ~4 frames of drift are unrelated 1-frame rounding noise present throughout, not part of this bug).
- **both dropped ranges were independently verified to work correctly** in an earlier, smaller call: they are members of a 60-range set applied successfully earlier the same session (that result was checked byte-for-byte: correct duration, correct clip count, correct final structure). The same two ranges, same source file, same absolute frame numbers, fail only once the batch grows to 87 ranges — so the defect is a function of the LARGER/differently-composed batch, not of anything intrinsic to those two ranges' own frame numbers.
- **where it must live, from reading the code:** `case 'ripple_delete_ranges'` (`timeline.ts`) calls `mergeFrameRanges(op.ranges)` then iterates back-to-front calling `rippleDeleteOneRange` per merged range. `rippleDeleteOneRange` itself has an early-return in its clip-removal loop — `if (after === next) return next;` — documented as "Refused (locked track, or a link member on one). Stop rather than spin" — which silently abandons the REST of that one range's own removal work (and skips `remove_gap` entirely) if a single `applyOp({kind:'remove',...})` call is refused for any reason, with the refusal never surfaced to the batch caller. Not yet confirmed whether this specific early-return is what fires for these two ranges, or whether the defect is instead in `mergeFrameRanges`'s merge/sort logic misbehaving on this particular 87-entry input, or in cumulative frame-shift arithmetic drifting by the time the back-to-front loop reaches these two positions (list indices 37 and 67 of the sorted 87 — not obviously significant, noted for whoever investigates).
- **not fixed here.** This needs real debugging (reproduce with the exact 87-range list — preserved in this session's own investigation, available on request — under a debugger or with added tracing, not guessed at from reading alone) before choosing a fix: whichever internal call is being silently refused needs to either (a) not be refusable under these real conditions (the actual root state issue), or (b) have its refusal surfaced all the way up to `editor_ripple_delete_ranges`'s own return value — a caller must never see `"ok": true` for a batch that didn't fully apply.
- **workaround used for tonight's real edit, disclosed as a workaround per this repo's own standing rule, not presented as a fix:** the coordinating session split the same total edit into two smaller `editor_ripple_delete_ranges` calls (the original working 60-range set, then a second, separate call for the remaining ~27 new ranges against the already-cut timeline) rather than one 87-range call, and verified each call's actual result against its own expected frame arithmetic before trusting it. This is not a fix for the underlying defect and does not establish any safe batch size — it only avoided the SPECIFIC combination that was seen to fail once. **Superseded by the fix below — no longer needed.**

### Root cause (2026-09-19) — reproduced, not inferred

- **Searched before fixing, and what the search ruled OUT.** The three suspects this entry named were each tested empirically against the real reducer. `mergeFrameRanges` misbehaving on an 87-entry input: **ruled out** — merging is union-preserving, and 200 random 87-range batches over a 16,475-frame single clip came back with the frame-level union exactly right. Cumulative frame-shift/rounding drift at high frame numbers: **ruled out** — same 87-range fuzz at 24fps, at 24000/1001, and with a clip whose `source_fps` is deliberately a hair off the project rate (a probe-rounded `23.976` against a `24000/1001` timeline), all clean; the round-trip through `timelineFramesToSource` only diverges for a rate ratio far larger than any real probe error. A single video track cannot reproduce this bug at all: **every combination** of two ranges on a 24-frame clip, on an already-3-clip track, and as an A/V-linked pair (exhaustive, not sampled) applies correctly.
- **What actually reproduces it: a SECOND track.** Two independent mechanisms, both real, both reproduced as tests that fail against the pre-fix reducer:
  - **a refused gap close — the one that matches this entry's own numbers.** Fixture: a 1000-frame clip on track 0, a sync-locked graphic on track 1 covering `[380, 600)`, and three ranges `[100,150) [450,500) [700,750)`. The middle range's ripple would have to close a gap ending at frame 500, which the graphic straddles, so `remove_gap` is refused — **B-033's own reject-on-straddle contract working exactly as designed**, the same rule B-227 found for `remove_gap`'s own handler. Pre-fix result, measured: `0..100 / 100..400 / 450..650 / 650..900` — the material *was* cut, the hole was *not* closed, the timeline came out **50 frames longer than the arithmetic union implies**, and the call reported success. That is B-197's live signature to the frame: "630 frames longer than the union" with a clip count that looks as though everything applied (each such range still yields one net new clip, exactly like a successful one), which is also why the live post-mortem's frame-coverage brute force read it as "two ranges not applied at all."
  - **a refused razor.** Fixture: a J-cut A/V pair (video `[0,1000)`, its linked audio `[600,1000)`), ranges `[100,150)` and `[700,750)`. D-129 refuses to split a link group at a frame that is not strictly inside every member, so the first range's `split` is refused; nothing is then wholly inside it, nothing is removed, and there is no gap to close — **the range vanishes from the batch entirely** while the other one applies, so the timeline changes and the handler's reference-equality check reports `{ok: true}`. This is the shape the entry's title describes.
- **The `if (after === next) return next;` line this entry pointed at is real but was NOT the trigger.** It fires only when `remove` is refused outright (a locked track holding a link partner), and that refuses *every* range of a single-track batch, so the old backstop already caught it as a total no-op. The bug lived in the two paths either side of it.
- **A fourth path, found by enumeration rather than reproduction, and fixed as well:** a `remove` that empties a track prunes it, which renumbers every later track — and the batch loop went on using the raw index, so the remaining ranges of the batch could cut a **different track**. It now follows the edited track by a clip it still owns.
- **fix (D-361):** `applyRippleDeleteRanges` — the whole batch as one exported pure function returning `{timeline, results}`, one `{start, end, applied, reason?}` per merged range. `applyOp`'s case is now that function and nothing else, and both callers run it as a dry run to learn the outcome: `editor_ripple_delete_ranges` answers `ok: false` with `applied`/`requested`/`skipped[{startFrame, endFrame, reason}]` when any range did not land, and the Recut panel's Cut button says `Cut 85 of 87 ranges — the other 2 could not be cut and were left untouched: …` instead of its old unconditional notice. A range that cannot complete now **rolls back** rather than half-applying, so a refused cut leaves no un-closed hole and no orphan split boundaries. `checkSplit`/`checkRemove` join `checkRemoveGap`/`checkTrim` as shared, exported precondition functions (B-227's pattern) so the reasons come from the rules themselves; none of D-129/B-033's actual behaviour changed.
- **verification:** 7 new tests in `rippleDeleteRanges.test.ts` (both reproductions above, one-result-per-merged-range, a cut that legitimately runs off the end of the track, a range describing no material, a locked track, and reducer/function agreement) + 3 in `timeline.test.ts` for `checkSplit`/`checkRemove`. The straddle reproduction was **confirmed non-vacuous against the pre-fix reducer** (restored `timeline.ts` from `HEAD`, ran it, got the un-closed 50-frame gap above). Full `@apelles/editor` suite **114 files / 2084 tests green**; `tsc -p packages/editor` unchanged at the 3 pre-existing `RecutPanel.dom.test.tsx`/`recutSweep.test.ts` fixture-typing errors (D-349's, none in any file this touched), `tsc -p app` unchanged at its 65 pre-existing i18n errors with **zero** from `packages/editor`; MCP parity corpus re-captured (one line changed, this tool's description) and `cargo test -p apelles-mcp --test parity` 5/5, `cargo fmt`/`clippy` clean.
- **no Rust mirror to keep in step:** `crates/apelles-timeline` has no batched ripple-delete op at all — this batching exists only in the TS reducer (D-318). The three primitives it composes (`split`/`remove`/`remove_gap`) keep their Rust twins' behaviour exactly; only the TS side's *reporting* and per-range rollback changed.
